paragraphs.text: Dear sisters and elders, I hope you are making this a great day through your agency and the control of your attitude. This wise saying is especially true in times like this. Quote, "most people are about as happy as they make up their minds to be," close quote.

As I worked on the habits material over the weekend, I quickly could see that to share it with you would be very, very hard unless I had visuals to use so that you could see the different behavior models that have to be understood before you can see clearly how to make changes in your behavior and dropping those bad habits and building good ones.

I'll have to think about how to do this a little more. And as soon as I have a plan, I will bring the learning to you, maybe in a couple of weeks. For this week, which is already busy with zone interviews, I'll share some learnings that are more easily understood and more easily prepared for me or by me, I should say. Anyway, let's get on with that.

Some years ago, I read a great novel about a Russian count or a nobleman who was caught up in the Communist Revolution that swept through Russia in the 1930s. So while many of the events told in the book really happened, this book was fiction. The story of the count was not real, but still there were many great things I learned from reading the novel. It was a great read. I loved it.

The story went like this. This rich young man, the count, was a good person. He was kind to people, kind to the servants that worked in his household and worked on his farm. Everybody liked him. They respected him. He wasn't like many people who have power, always putting themselves above others. He stayed humble and he was always willing to learn no matter who he was with.

One day, he decided to travel to Moscow to visit friends and enjoy the city. He stayed at the famous and luxurious Metropole Hotel. It was the finest hotel in Moscow and actually still is by most accounts. He stayed there often. He came to Moscow often. But he was there at that hotel so many times that he had a permanent suite that was constantly reserved just for him. He was rich.

Now, while he was in Moscow, he went out with his friends to the opera, to the ballet, to dinner parties and receptions. He was having a wonderful time. And then without warning, the revolution happened. The government was toppled. A new government came in.

And since the count was a member of the nobility, he was a part of the Tsar's government. He was automatically suspected of being against the communists. But since he had been such a good and kind person, he was not immediately arrested and killed like many of the other nobility.

He stayed in his suite at the Metropole Hotel not sure what was going to happen, but peaceful about the fact that he knew he had always been a good and generous person. And he certainly knew that there were many, many of his fellow noblemen that had been pretty terrible to their people so he could understand and sympathize a little bit with this change in government.

Well, one day the authorities did come for him. And they told him that while they wanted to arrest him, he had some friends in the new government. And so he wasn't free to go because there was a power struggle in the government about him and many other things. And they said that he had to stay inside the hotel and not step one foot outside of it, or he would be arrested and tried for treason and probably shot dead.

He was surprised by this and a bit discouraged, but he did as he was told. A few weeks went by and because he had lots of money, he was able to eat very well at the wonderful restaurants inside the hotel. He couldn't go out, but his true friends would sometimes come by and visit him. It wasn't his best choice of life, but he was okay with it and he maintained a good attitude.

After a while, the authorities came again. And this time they took all of the money that he had that they could find. And they told him that they'd taken all of his lands in the family home. The government had taken everything. They told him he had some friends still in the government, so they wouldn't arrest him. But they didn't think it was right that he should be living in this fancy suite. And so they moved him to the janitor's storage room.

Just a tiny little room where there was enough room for a small little cot, a little bed, and a little place for his clothes, and that was it. Still, he couldn't step one foot outside the hotel or he would be arrested, so he stayed. Now, he wasn't too happy about this situation, but again, he chose to be cheerful and look for the good.

He was still alive and many of his friends were no longer alive, so that was something to be thankful for. He was in a warm place and not outside in the freezing Moscow winter, so that was something to be thankful for. He still had a little money that he had hidden so he could still eat a little, so that was something to be thankful for.

However, he knew that his money wouldn't last too much longer. He knew that his enemies wanted him to be forced to leave, and then they could arrest him no matter about the friends he had. What should he do? As a member of the nobility, he had never had to have a job before.

But since he had always been so nice to people, he had many friends among the workers in the hotel. He shared his concerns with a few of them and they said, well, you know so much about fine dining and great manners and culture. Why don't you apply to be a waiter at the restaurant?

Now, many people would have rejected that. He was a count, but because he was humble, he thought that was a great idea. He got the job and was able to make enough to eat, and he enjoyed the work and he did a great job with it. He didn't worry about what he used to be. He just worked hard to be the best waiter in the restaurant. Eventually, he became the head waiter.

Many of the high officials of the new government came to the restaurant to eat, and they knew who he was. They didn't treat him too well because of that, but he was always courteous and professional in response to whatever they did. Eventually, many of these officials also became his friends. They couldn't change his fate, but they could show their respect for him in other ways, which they did.

Life went on in this way for 20 years, and eventually, he was able to get back to his home, and along the way, however, he helped so many people live a better life and see the good in the world around them.

As I thought about this book, it helped me to think differently about this quarantine that we're experiencing. One of the best lines in the book has become a quote that I review regularly. It goes like this, quote, "If you don't master your circumstances, they will master you," close quote.

The count showed me how, but I already knew it, and that is through kindness and long suffering, and treating people the way you would like them to treat you. Like the people of Alma in the land of Helam, we need to seek the Lord's help with our challenges, but we also need to be willing to submit ourselves cheerfully and with patience to all the will of the Lord.

As we learn how to do this, we turn our afflictions into our blessings, and we become a light to all who are around us. Elders and sisters, be cheerful and confident. Express your faith and your hope to all who will listen to you. Family, fellow missionaries, members, and our friends, express it to all of them. As you do so, you will be mastering your circumstances, and life will become even more wonderful for you. God bless you. Good night. We love you.
